extracted.intended_audience: British political leaders, legislators, and the educated public skeptical of the French Revolution
extracted.subtask_description: An 18th-century polemical essay arguing against revolutionary reorganization of government and laying out normative criteria for legitimate representation, the composition of legislatures, and the preservation of property and social order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness of those elevated to supreme authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Supreme authority should not be vested in men 'not taught habitually to respect themselves' or previously of humble station who suddenly acquire power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues such men will be intoxicated by sudden greatness, pursue private interests at public expense, and are likely to join in creating a 'litigious constitution' to obtain lucrative offices. Anti-pattern: elevating individuals from obscure, contentious backgrounds without prior probative trials of character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid predominance of professional factions (especially lawyers)
rubrics_metrics.description: A legislature should not be dominated by those formed by professional and faculty habits (e.g., lawyers), because their excellence in particular functions may disqualify them for general statesmanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When lawyers preponderate, their recurrent, narrow employment cripples comprehension of mixed public affairs. Example/contrast: the British Commons contains varied elements that counterbalance professional narrowness; a body dominated by lawyers risks governance driven by chicane rather than the public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional experience (medicine, law, commerce) is no substitute for statesmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Professions like medicine or commerce do not naturally form qualified statesmen; their training and habitual concerns are inadequate for legislating a nation's complex interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke notes doctors and traders lack the comprehensive view necessary for forming constitutions; their participation should not preponderate. Anti-pattern: treating faculty competence within a trade as qualification for broad legislative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative bodies must include natural landed interest
rubrics_metrics.description: A true representation of the state must represent ability and property, particularly the landed interest, which stabilizes property and society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke emphasizes that landed proprietors act as ballast for the commonwealth and protect both large and lesser properties. Warning: assemblies lacking landed representation (like the Tiers État as described) will undermine property stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for constitutional restraints and counterpoises
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative power should be constrained by fundamental laws, conventions, usage, counterbalancing institutions (e.g., House of Lords, Crown), and established practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke contrasts the British constitutional checks with the unbounded power of the French National Assembly, arguing absence of restraints makes a body dangerously able to remake constitution to its designs. Scoring note: bodies with fixed constraints are preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for government: virtue and wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: The only true qualifications for government are virtue and wisdom (actual or presumptive), not blood, titles, or merely mean occupations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While Burke rejects exclusive privilege by birth, he insists that low education or sordid occupations are not preferable titles to command. Merit must be tested; virtue is proven through difficulty and struggle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit should be rare and subject to probation
rubrics_metrics.description: The advent to eminence and power from obscure condition should not be made too easy; rare merit should pass through some probation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'temple of honor' ought to be seated on an eminence; virtue is 'never tried but by some difficulty and some struggle.' Anti-pattern: instantaneous elevation by sortition/rotation without proof of capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against sortition/rotation/lot for offices of extensive responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Appointment by lot, rotation, or indiscriminate modes of election are generally unsuitable for governments concerned with extensive objects because they do not select men according to duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such methods lack tendency to match a person's capacities to the duty required; they can displace tested ability. Burke asserts 'no rotation, no appointment by lot... can be generally good' for such governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation must reflect ability as well as property
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper representation is one that embodies both the property-holding and the active ability required to govern; property alone is sluggish and must be predominant in the representation to be safe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because ability is active and property inert, property must be overrepresented to defend itself. Failure to represent large property masses weakens defense of property rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property's concentrated masses protect smaller holdings
rubrics_metrics.description: Large accumulations of property form a natural rampart protecting lesser properties; diffusion weakens defensive power and invites rapacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues that when property is widely diffused, individuals cannot accurately calculate the small share they'd gain by plunder, making them susceptible to leaders who promise redistribution. Policy implication: maintain structures that keep significant property concentrations safeguarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetuation of family property is vital to social stability
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to perpetuate property in families is among the most valuable conditions for the perpetuation of society; hereditary property-holders are natural securities for transmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions like a House of Peers (hereditary) are defended as final judges of property issues. Guidance warns against policies that undermine hereditary transmission without adequate safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levelling undermines natural social order and does not equalize
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to 'level' society by abolishing distinctions do not equalize but pervert the natural order: some descriptions of citizens must be uppermost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke contends levellers 'only change and pervert the natural order' and create instability by placing unsuited groups into roles that require different capacities (e.g., guild-style associations ruling a nation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain occupations are unsuitable as bases for ruling authority
rubrics_metrics.description: While honest employments are not disgraceful, occupations such as hair-dresser or tallow-chandler are not matters of honor and should not be permitted to rule the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke concedes that no honest employment should suffer oppression, but warns the state 'suffers oppression, if such as they ... are permitted to rule.' He frames this as conflict with natural distinctions necessary for governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of representative assemblies must guard against instruments of plunder
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemblies composed chiefly of men who would work as instruments (e.g., curates, country attorneys, money-jobbers) rather than controllers will be prone to ignorance, rashness, presumption, and plunder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke describes how curates, country attorneys, and jobbers lack worldly experience and are apt to be guided by others or by envy—leading to collective decisions that endanger property and order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware metropolitan domination over provinces in republican reorganization
rubrics_metrics.description: A republican system that fragments a nation into many municipalities risks a dominant capital (e.g., Paris) monopolizing power and spoils, making coherent national governance impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke predicts that eighty-three independent municipalities cannot be governed as one body and that the 'republic of Paris' would attempt to perpetuate despotism through paper circulation and monopolization of spoils. Practical warning: federative fragmentation without strong integrative institutions is unstable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutionary claim that representation equals legitimacy is dangerous
rubrics_metrics.description: To assert that popular representation is the sole source of legitimacy delegitimizes existing institutions (lords, crown, revolutions themselves) and provides philosophical pretext for dismantling established orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke critiques the revolutionists' doctrine that without representation no government is legitimate; he points out this principle would render the Revolution itself baseless and justify wholesale destruction of precedents and charters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic convention limits natural rights within civil society
rubrics_metrics.description: Rights of uncovenanted (natural) man do not wholly transfer into civil society; civil society is founded on convention which necessarily limits and modifies individual claims (e.g., no man should be judge in his own cause).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke stresses that entering civil society requires abdicating certain natural rights—self-government and self-defense—for the rule of law. This is a foundational principle for legitimate legal authority and procedural fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience, precedent, and gradual reform should be valued over sweeping abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Political metaphysics and abstract rights ('the rights of men' as absolute) that despise experience, precedents, charters, and established laws are perilous when they are used to justify large-scale upheaval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke insists that experience is the 'wisdom of unlettered men' and that despising historical continuity invites catastrophic consequences. Anti-pattern: treating theoretical purity as sufficient ground for revolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political leaders should not seek power for mere domination or plunder
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who lead by seeking the overthrow of orders for private advantage—e.g., turbulent men of rank inflated with pride, or money-jobbers changing paper wealth into land—will pursue the spoil of others rather than the common good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke warns that such leaders will encourage envy, revenge, and sweeping redistribution to reward new followers; historical examples include persons who betrayed their order and then joined rebellions they had helped create.
